messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Harrison's eyes still scan the room with a habituated air of vigilance, a trait honed from years as a combat pilot. But it wasn't the wars he fought that left him with this perpetual sense of threat; it was the battles he endured in his own home. The physical abuse he suffered at the hands of his romantic partner has left an indelible mark on his life. The memories of those violent encounters are still vivid, and Harrison has developed a keen sensitivity to triggers that transport him back to those moments. The smell of alcohol, for instance, can instantly evoke the image of his abuser's face, contorted in anger. Seeing someone who resembles his former partner can also send his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. And physical touch – even a gentle pat on the back or an innocuous brush against a stranger's arm – can make him recoil as if expecting a blow. To cope with these triggers, Harrison has developed maladaptive strategies that have become ingrained habits over time. He avoids anything that reminds him of his abuser, meticulously curating his surroundings to minimize potential reminders. Avoiding intimacy is another coping mechanism; Harrison finds it difficult to form close relationships or even allow himself to feel a deep emotional connection with others. Suppressing anger has also become second nature – he never allows himself to express this emotion, fearing that doing so might unleash the same kind of violence he suffered. As a result of these avoidance strategies, Harrison's world has grown smaller and more isolating. His social circle has shrunk significantly since his partner passed away, leaving him feeling lonely but also relieved to be free from the constant stress of being on guard around others. Yet, this very isolation exacerbates his threat perception. He lies awake at night, vigilant for sounds that might signal an intruder – even though he lives in a secure neighborhood with minimal crime. His hypervigilance has become so all-consuming that Harrison can't shake the feeling of being constantly "on guard," watching and waiting for potential threats to materialize. Even innocuous stimuli like the sound of footsteps outside his apartment or the sight of an unfamiliar face on the street can set off a chain reaction of physical reactivity – rapid heartbeat, tense muscles, and the familiar knot in his stomach. As Harrison navigates this complex web of triggers, maladaptive strategies, and perceived threats, it's clear that these elements are self-reinforcing. Avoiding intimacy, for instance, has led to increased isolation, which in turn heightens his sense of threat and vulnerability – making him even more likely to avoid social interactions or form meaningful connections with others. This cycle is one he struggles to break free from. Harrison's recent struggles with sleep have finally prompted him to seek help. The physical toll of constant vigilance has become too much to bear, and the isolation has grown unbearable. As he sits in his therapist's office, he's most afraid that he'll never be able to shake this perpetual sense of threat – that he'll be forever trapped in this cycle of hypervigilance and avoidance. Yet, it's also here that Harrison begins to see a glimmer of hope: the possibility of confronting these maladaptive strategies head-on and slowly rebuilding his life around new, healthier patterns of thought and behavior.
